From the Bridge

From the Commanding Officer

Shipmates,

It is my pleasure to welcome you to the first issue of the relaunched Voice Pipe.

The Voice Pipe has a long history at HMCS Tecumseh. For many years, earlier editions helped share news, recognize accomplishments, and capture something of the life of the ship’s company. Bringing it back gives us an opportunity to continue that tradition in a form suited to today’s Naval Reserve.

Tecumseh is a busy ship. Throughout the year, members of our ship’s company train, deploy, support operations and exercises, develop new skills, serve our community, and represent the Royal Canadian Navy across Canada and around the world. Much of that work happens beyond the view of the rest of the unit. The Voice Pipe gives us a place to share those experiences.

It is also an opportunity to recognize the people who make Tecumseh what it is. Every member of the ship’s company has a perspective worth sharing, whether it comes from an exercise, a course, a deployment, an interesting experience at the unit, or simply something others might enjoy knowing.

In these pages, we will also look back. Tecumseh has been part of Calgary for more than a century, and generations of sailors have contributed to the history and traditions we inherit today. Remembering their stories helps us understand our own place in that continuing history.

Most importantly, I hope the Voice Pipe becomes a publication created by and for the ship’s company. I encourage you to read it, contribute to it, and help us tell the stories of the people who serve at Tecumseh today.

Thank you to everyone who has contributed to this first issue, and to those who have helped bring the Voice Pipe back to life.

Cdr Anna Kocot, CD
Commanding Officer
HMCS TECUMSEH

The Masthead

A Letter from the Editor

The Voice Pipe — Then and Now, 1957–2026

Although the origins of the original Voice Pipe newsletter have been lost in the sands of time, the evidence that we do have, including my personal recollection and conversations with other members, indicates that the newsletter was around from its earliest days in the 1950s until well into the 1990s. It was a regular part of life at Tecumseh, a welcome source of news about the unit, its people and its activities—and an opportunity for members to tell their own stories.

From exercises and deployments to mess dinners, sporting events, family milestones and everyday happenings, the original publication helped keep the ship's company informed and connected. It offered room for both accomplishments and good-natured humour, reflecting the camaraderie that makes naval service memorable.

The Wren's Mess column offers a particularly fitting reminder of why those stories matter. Describing a successful social evening, its writer reflected on the value of getting together, building esprit de corps and putting faces to names. The Wren's Mess may be long gone, but the issues of the day, the sense of connection we share, and the desire to be a part of a larger community remain familiar, even now.

That is the tradition we hope to revive. The new Voice Pipe is a place to celebrate our people, our accomplishments, and the enjoyable experiences that connect us to one another and to our shared service. It is also a way to preserve today's stories for future members of Tecumseh.

How we produce and deliver the newsletter will continue to evolve. We will look for ways to make it accessible, useful and enjoyable, learning from each issue and adapting as we go. Some ideas will work better than others, and we will improve the publication with experience and feedback.

Above all, its future depends on contributions from the ship's company. The best stories come from the people who lived them. We hope that today's members will come to value this renewed Voice Pipe as earlier generations valued theirs—and that it will continue for years to come.

The design may have changed, but the purpose remains: to share our stories, celebrate our people, and keep the ship's company connected.

Capt Mike Mirtle, CD · Unit Historian, HMCS TECUMSEH

Around the Unit

Tecumseh on the Water: Ghost Lake Ops

Small-boat training, changing weather and a weekend of teamwork.

Story and photographs by Anonymous Contributor · 26–27 September 2026

“Stand by for air support … over,” we radioed out to one of our small boats from the Operations Centre (OpsCen). We had observed a small aircraft flying overhead and thought our boat crew might appreciate our humour. They laughed about it when they returned to the jetty, telling us that they appreciated the integration of the real-world aircraft into our training exercise.

While, of course, the plane continued on its flight path and did not provide air support to our small boat, this is just one of many examples of how Ghost Lake provided us with opportunities to integrate real-world observations into our Small Boat Exercise (SBEX) training scenario.

This year, a Domestic Operations scenario was integrated into our start-of-year SBEX. Many members of TEC have deployed on OP LENTUS (domestic disaster response) assignments supporting forest fire response from the ground. The command team who planned the SBEX used the experiences of those members to develop taskings that may be given to a small watercraft in a similar forest fire response.

Over the two-day exercise, we experienced working under a mock Incident Command System (ICS) and ran a small intelligence cell focused on current and future operations. Our NavComms also experienced an endless flow of radio traffic and were very much up to the challenge!

Roles for our small boats included surveying of (pretend) fires from the water, reporting (fake) smoke conditions back to the OpsCen, and a variety of pretend encounters with more complex emergencies such as mock train derailments, emergency civilian situations, and evacuation notifications.

We even got to keep a Canadian Navy tradition alive with 10 o’clock soup (though soup was served at lunch, as everyone was on a boat by 10 o’clock!).

We were quite cold on the first day of the exercise, but the second day of the SBEX ended up over 20 degrees Celsius! Day two, however, started with extremely thick, low fog cover and provided very realistic “train how we fight” practice, as boats were launched and set off from the jetty in less-than-ideal visibility. The fog provided an exceptionally realistic experience of what conditions could be like in a forest fire response setting with heavy smoke.

While the SBEX was undoubtedly a fun time that built skills and camaraderie, it was also extremely successful in providing a training environment for all trades, both land-based and sea-going.

“I was able to see firsthand how intelligence operators work in the field. I’ll be happy to do another one again if given the opportunity.” — S3 Tran, OpsCen participant

The good news is that we will all soon have the opportunity to participate in more SBEXs and scenario-based training, as HMCS Tecumseh is in the early stages of planning more exercises come spring!

While our weekend at Ghost Lake had some questionable weather on the first day, we ended our second day in +20-degree sunshine, having successfully completed dynamic training exercises and built lasting friendships that will carry us through the rest of our Navy careers.

See you at the next SBEX!!

A Sailor's Life

Five Weeks at RIMPAC 2026

A personal perspective from inside a multinational maritime task force

Story and Pictures by: Lt(N) M.S. Podorieszach

From June to July 2026, I had the opportunity to participate in Rim of the Pacific (RIMPAC) 2026 for five weeks as the Deputy Director of Current Operations within the Commander Combined Task Force (CCTF) group. This role provided a unique perspective on the world's largest multinational maritime exercise and offered valuable experience working alongside allied and partner nations in both planning and execution of complex operations.

Learning alongside partner nations

During the harbour phase in Hawaii, while participating ships remained in port, I attended a number of professional development and exercise preparation activities. These included attending a legal symposium that examined emerging trends in international maritime law, participating in information warfare sessions and supporting the humanitarian assistance and disaster response portion of the exercise. These activities highlighted the broad spectrum of missions modern naval forces must be prepared to conduct beyond traditional warfare.

Coordinating a combined force

A key aspect of my role was understanding and supporting the relationship between the Combined Task Force Commander (CCTF), the Combined Force Maritime Component Commander (CFMCC), and the air and special operations commands. The CCTF provides overall operational direction for the exercise, while the CFMCC coordinates maritime operations and assigns tasks to naval forces. Air and special operations components operate within the commander's intent, integrating their capabilities to achieve common objectives across the battlespace. Effective coordination between these commands was essential to ensure a synchronized multinational response to the scenarios presented throughout the exercise.

From harbour to sea

The sea phase marked the transition to operational training, with approximately 30 vessels deploying at sea. Participating nations included Canada, the United States, Australia, Japan, South Korea, Chile, Mexico, New Zealand, Peru, the Philippines, Singapore, and several other partner nations. Canada's contribution included HMCS Ottawa, HMCS Regina, HMCS Cornerbrook, and MV Asterix, which played important roles in demonstrating Canadian maritime capability including the final shot that sank a former US naval ship.

The at-sea portion of RIMPAC was conducted through a realistic fictional scenario involving conventional military threats, natural disasters, and an unconventional paramilitary or terrorist organization attempting to destabilize the region through a coup. Maritime, air, amphibious, and special operations forces worked together to train in a dynamic environment that required continuous coordination and adaptation.

The watch never stops

Within the CCTF headquarters, a 24-hour watch floor monitored and coordinated both exercise events and real-world requirements. In addition to managing the exercise scenario, the watch team responded to several actual emergencies involving participating vessels and civilian vessels, demonstrating the importance of maintaining operational awareness and readiness while conducting large-scale multinational operations. The experience provided invaluable insight into coalition command and control, multinational interoperability, and the challenges associated with coordinating complex maritime operations on a global scale.

Get to Know... Our Coxswain

PO1 Greg Hofer, CD

Coxswain, HMCS TECUMSEH

Hometown: Sundre, Alberta
Joined the CAF: 15 July 1999, Calgary
Joined HMCS TECUMSEH: 5 October 2021

A Career of Service

Originally from Sundre, Alberta, Petty Officer 1st Class Greg Hofer joined the Canadian Armed Forces on 15 July 1999, beginning his career in the Regular Force as a Steward.

Over more than 27 years of service, PO1 Hofer has accumulated extensive operational experience, including three major deployments aboard HMCS Winnipeg, deployments involving HMCS Calgary, HMCS Vancouver, and HMCS Ville de Québec, and a deployment to Afghanistan.

His specialized qualifications include Close Protection Operator and Maritime Tactical Operator, reflecting a career encompassing both traditional naval service and specialized operational roles.

PO1 Hofer joined HMCS TECUMSEH on 5 October 2021. His responsibilities at the unit have included Facility Manager, Training Coordinator, and Coxswain. He currently serves as a GSNCO with the Naval Reserve.

Leadership and Priorities

As Coxswain, PO1 Hofer identifies his primary responsibilities as representing the unit's non-commissioned members and supporting the Chain of Command to the best of his ability.

His approach emphasizes professional development, resilience, teamwork, and ensuring that sailors have the support they need to succeed.

A Message from the Coxswain

Sailors,

As the face of modern warfare continues to change, so must we. The Royal Canadian Navy is evolving to meet new challenges, and I expect every member of this ship's company to adapt, remain resilient, and rise to meet those demands with confidence and professionalism.

Challenges are inevitable, but they are also opportunities to grow. I encourage each of you to embrace them, push your limits, and strive to be better every day.

Know that you are not expected to carry these burdens alone. As your Coxswain, I am here to support you, advocate for you, and help you succeed.

My goal is simple: to see every sailor challenged, developed, and ultimately successful.

Together, through teamwork, determination, and mutual support, we will continue to strengthen our ship's company and be ready for whatever the future brings.

PO1 Greg Hofer, CD
Coxswain, HMCS TECUMSEH

Naval Trivia

Why Soup at 1000?

The Royal Canadian Navy’s 10 O’Clock Soup Tradition

Few naval traditions are as simple, or as warmly regarded, as the Royal Canadian Navy’s custom of serving soup at the morning Stand Easy. At approximately 1000 each working day, sailors take a welcome break from their duties and gather for a hot bowl of soup. Whether aboard ship or at a shore establishment, this modest ritual provides an opportunity to warm up, recharge, and enjoy a few moments of camaraderie with shipmates.

Although it feels like a tradition that has been around forever, the widespread practice of serving soup at 1000 appears to be relatively recent. According to an article published in Lookout in August 2022, archival photographs show sailors enjoying soup aboard HMCS Restigouche, a destroyer commissioned in 1958. By the mid-1970s, soup was being served during Stand Easy at the Osbourne Head Gunnery Range in Nova Scotia. The practice became increasingly common aboard East Coast ships during the early 1980s, was nearly universal there by the middle of that decade, and had spread to the West Coast fleet by the mid-1990s.

There are several practical reasons for the tradition’s popularity. A hot bowl of soup is particularly welcome during cold or wet weather, and it provides nourishment and hydration during a busy working day. For the galley staff, soup is economical, versatile, and an excellent way to make use of available ingredients. But perhaps its greatest value is social. Like many naval customs, 10 o’clock soup brings sailors together, providing a regular opportunity to share stories, exchange news, and strengthen the bonds that make a ship’s company more than simply a collection of individuals.

The tradition also reflects the diversity of today’s Navy. In her Lookout article, S1 Marianne Mojica of HMCS Regina shared her recipe for Chicken Tinola, a Filipino soup passed down through her family. It is a fitting reminder that naval traditions are not necessarily fixed in the past; they continue to evolve as new generations of sailors bring their own experiences and cultures to the mess deck. Whether it’s a traditional chowder, a hearty vegetable soup, or a family favourite, the humble bowl of soup remains one of the RCN’s most enjoyable customs.

Further reading: Canadian Navy’s 10 o’clock soup tradition — Lookout, 18 August 2022

From the Galley

HMCS Haida Clam Chowder · 1948

A recipe from the 1948 RCN Recipe Manual, reproduced by Parks Canada.

A former HMCS Haida sailor recalled that the appearance of clam chowder on the menu meant it was Friday. The historical recipe uses clams, salt pork, potatoes, onions, milk, flour and thyme, and is served with navy or soda biscuits.

Read the complete original recipe: Parks Canada — HMCS Haida Clam Chowder.

Have a favourite soup recipe? Send it in for a future edition of The Voice Pipe . A family favourite, a galley memory or a recipe with a naval connection would all be welcome.

Your Voice Pipe

Have a Story to Tell?

The history of Tecumseh has always been written, in part, by its own people. We invite today's ship's company to contribute news, photographs, training experiences, professional achievements, personal stories, historical finds, humour and favourite recipes.

You do not need to write a polished article. A few notes, a photograph with a caption, or an idea for a story can be a useful starting point.

Have something to contribute? Contact the Unit Historian about a story, photograph, historical item or recipe for a future issue: Capt Mike Mirtle <michael.mirtle@ecn.forces.gc.ca>

A Note About Public Distribution

The Voice Pipe is published online at voicepipe.ca and is freely accessible to the public. By submitting material for consideration, contributors acknowledge that approved articles and photographs may be published and shared publicly.

Please ensure submissions contain no sensitive or restricted information and that appropriate permission has been obtained to share photographs and other material.

All submissions are subject to editorial review and approval before publication.

Your ship. Your stories. Your Voice Pipe.
